sections.text: The Self of him who is self-controlled, and has attained peace is equally unmoved by heat or cold, pleasure or pain, honour or dishonour.
He who desires nothing but wisdom and spiritual insight, who has conquered his senses and who looks with the same eye upon a lump of earth, a stone or fine gold, is a real saint.
He looks impartially on all - lover, friend or foe; indifferent or hostile; alien or relative; virtuous or sinful.

Unlike a car with its users manual, we are born without instructions on how to live. We experience lifes vicissitudes without a so-called users manual. The Gita has been described as such a guide.
So last time we have seen that the advice from Bhagavad Gita is: raise yourself by the self, dont let the self fall. We all really know in life that the only one who can truly help oneself is ones own self. Only my own efforts will raise me out of the situation Im in.
But the connotation here is: raise your lower self by the higher self. The self in me which remains constant throughout all these changes of birth and death -- as we have seen in chapter two -- is imperishable, immutable, untaintable. Let that self raise your lower self, which is suffering right now by its own limitations.
I cant stand limitations because my true nature is limitless. So the only thing I can do is let my higher self raise my lower self to the same level. Raise yourself by yourself.
Dont let yourself fall. Dont let your lower self go even further down. And thats because it says the higher self is a friend of the lower self.
When this lower self is conquered by the higher self, when the lower self starts identifying with the higher self, recognizing its existence, there is something beyond my this day to day life which I live. There is something beyond the life which I consider started at my birth and will end at my death. When I start recognizing this and make that higher self a friend of this lower self, Ill be able to pull the lower self out of its present state of misery.
But it said the same self, higher self, can be the enemy of the lower self. If my ego fails to recognize that there is something beyond my this limited self, then the same higher self will act as if its enemy because it will let you go down further and further into this misery. By empowering you to do the wrong thing.
Higher self will empower you to do whatever you wish you to do. If the ego goes down into the lower and lower plane of existence, it will be empowered by the same higher self. Just as a car out of control is empowered by the same gas which is in the tank which was making it go straight on the road in a controlled fashion.
The same gas will power a disastrous wreck. So the advice was clearly: raise yourself by the self. But to do that, you have to have certain qualifications.
You have to make efforts to raise your lower self to a worthiness where it can start working with the higher self, start identifying with the higher self. The verses which we discussed -- 7, 8, and 9 -- describe the state of Yogarudha. One who has become master of his lower self is Yogarudha.
We have seen two stages: Arurukshu and Yogarudha. For someone who is desirous to gain control over his mind, body, and intellect, the advice was karma karanam uchyate -- keep working in this world with selfless motivation and you will achieve that. But once you reach that state where you have that control, then shamah karanam uchyate -- at that point, contemplation and meditation become the means to reach the higher level, to achieve the goal of eternal happiness.
We want to get out of the limitations. I want to be happy all the time. Bhagavan said it is absolutely possible, but only when you identify with the higher, not the lower.
You are the manifestation of the higher. But my identification right now is with the lower. As long as I dont identify with the lower, its limitations cannot affect me.
It is like when you go to the science museum or some place where there is funny mirror are there. I stand in front of it and I look like I have bloated 10 times than what I am today. Well, as long as I dont identify that image in the mirror, I am fine.
Everybody goes in a funny mirror and laugh at it. Because they are not identifying with the image they see in the mirror. They clearly identify with the self standing in front of the mirror.
Thats why they can laugh at it. But anyone who identifies with that distorted reflection cannot laugh. Our situation, Bhagavan says, like we are looking at ourselves in this funny mirror and looking at this miserable self.
And now we are in misery. But one who identifies with the real self standing in front of the mirror -- the higher self which makes this lower self possible -- is without any miseries. So the one who has achieved that sense of balance over himself has now become Yogarudha.
What will he gain? That is what we learned. In the last three verses it says: Jitatmanah prashantasya paramatma samahitah, shitoshna sukha duhkheshu tatha mana apamana yoh. Where do our problems lie? In the three levels we have seen here.
Physical condition is not comfortable -- the room is too hot or too cold. At the body level, I can be uncomfortable. At a mental level, I feel this is a good time or I dont have a good time -- things are not working out for me.
Then there is mana apamana yoh -- honor and dishonor. Intellectually, I feel that people are respecting me. I have achieved something -- or dishonor, theyre not respecting me.
All these are causes for pleasure and pain in life. But one who has achieved that Yogarudha state -- one who has recognized the existence of the higher self in him and started aligning himself with it -- for him, Prashantasya Paramatma: his self remains equanimous in all situations because he is not identifying with them. We wrongly understand that one who has achieved this state will not turn on the thermostat, because so what if it is uncomfortable. Well, thats sheer foolishness.
If I have the facility to adjust the temperature to my level of comfort, then I should do it. People often ask great teachers: , you talk about all this detachment, but when you come, people pick you up in Lexus and BMWs and Jaguars. Why dont you go with somebody who has a broken car?, My friend, Im a.
That doesnt mean Im completely stupid. As long as there is a more reliable and comfortable vehicle available, why should I choose one which is completely unreliable and uncomfortable? Thats a common sense. It has nothing to do with attachment or detachment. So we wrongly perceive that the person who has achieved this state has to suffer, that only then is he considered a true yogi.
But the teaching simply says the self in him, the higher self, is prasantasya -- always at equanimity. It is not disturbed by outside happenings. Whatever is happening at the body level, I see clearly that it is happening at the body level and let the body deal with it at its own capacity.
Whatever is happening at the mental level, I see clearly and let the mind deal with it. Whatever happens at the intellectual level, let my intellect deal with it at its own capacity. But I, the self -- the core of my being -- never get shaken by these happenings in this world.
Thats why I always say there are no riots when its 102 degrees outside in Richmond. We didnt have people throwing stones at Richmond City Hall. When the temperature hit 102 degrees, we expected that this can happen in summer.
Deal with it with the best situation we can create. So we all turned down our thermostat and let the air condition run as best as it can. But we didnt get upset, we didnt have anything to complain to because we knew that it is something beyond my control.
When a yogi becomes one with his higher self he sees all the occurring at the mental level, the physical level and the intellectual level occurring at the lower level of existence. But higher self is not involved and does not get attached to it. Its not affected by any of this thing.
So thats his fulfillment. Having become Yogarudha, he is no longer disturbed by small things which used to disturb him before. Previously, when it was hot, we complained all over the place.
Whenever things were not conducive, we complained. Now I can take it as it is and look at it as a transitory phase happening in my life, in my existence, and not get disturbed by it. The next verse says: Gnana vignana truptatma kutasthah vijitendriyah, yukta iti uchyate yogi sama loshta ashma kanchanah.
This is the verse I never understood when I was growing up. I have been learning Bhagavad Gita since I was about 18 years old, and I would think: what is my attitude in life if I become sama loshta ashma kanchanah -- equanimous toward a lump of clay, iron, and gold? Well, that means I have lost all kind of judgment in life! But it really doesnt say that. In your day-to-day transactions in this world, you do make differentiation between the usefulness or value of one thing or another.
But it does tell me that one who has achieved understanding, one who has the knowledge -- Gnana -- one who has learned from others, from books, from teachers, from listening, has received the knowledge. But that knowledge remains bookish until I apply it and make it my own. That becomes Vignana.
Thats what science labs are for. You learn in the classroom that H2O is water. Then you go to the lab and make it on your own with two molecules of hydrogen and one of oxygen, and say, Thats water! Now Im absolutely convinced.
Thats now my wisdom. Vignana visishtagnana. That only comes with self experience.
Experimenting what I have learned in my own life, I get wisdom. Thats why I didnt understand when I was 18. Now at 62, it is very clear, okay? Because I have gone through the experimentation of it in life.
So it says Gnana Vignana Truptatma Kutastha. Kutastha, I think, comes from the anvil in the smithy shop. The blacksmith is hammering something on that anvil -- both are made of iron.
But the one changes its shape while the anvil remains the same. So Kutastha means one who remains unshaken by whatever is happening. One who has control over his senses -- Yukta iti uchyate -- such a person is called fulfilled, harmonized, one who has achieved the sense of his self.
Sama loshta ashma kanchanah -- he sees the lump of clay, the iron, and the gold as the same. He sees each at its original value. What is the value of gold? What is the value of my house? Well, we put this place for lease or sell or whatever.
So what is the value? Well, I may want anything I want.

These verses describe the remarkable equanimity of one who has conquered the self: unmoved by heat or cold, pleasure or pain, honor or dishonor. But as wisely clarifies, this does not mean the yogi refuses to adjust the thermostat or chooses discomfort when comfort is available. The point is not to suffer needlessly, but to ensure that the core of your being - your inner peace - is not disturbed by external fluctuations. When it is 102 degrees outside, you may feel the heat, but you need not lose your mental equilibrium over it. The phrase sama-loshta-ashma-kanchanah - seeing equally a lump of clay, a stone, and gold - puzzled many seekers in their youth. Does wisdom mean losing all discrimination? Not at all. In practical transactions, gold is still more valuable than clay. But the wise person recognizes that the value is assigned, not inherent. Gold cannot give you lasting happiness any more than clay can. This understanding frees you from the tyranny of constantly chasing more valuable objects, believing they hold the key to your fulfillment. Reflect today on three categories of disturbance in your life: physical discomforts (heat, cold, illness), emotional fluctuations (good times, bad times), and intellectual wounds (feeling respected or disrespected). Which category most easily disturbs your peace? This is where your practice should focus. The goal is not to become insensitive, but to see clearly that these fluctuations are happening at the level of body, mind, or intellect - not at the level of your true self, which remains the unchanging witness.
